summary:
Imagine driving home during a harsh winter storm in Northeastern Ontario. Snow covers the road, visibility is limited, and the possibility of hidden or black ice creates uncertainty for drivers and their families. For communities that depend on these roads for work, school, and essential services, understanding changing road conditions from region to region can make a meaningful difference.

To address this challenge, we developed an affordable environmental monitoring system that combines NASA's historical Earth science data with real-time, localized measurements. Using temperature, humidity, and ultrasonic sensors connected to a microcontroller, our system monitors atmospheric conditions and estimates snow accumulation on road surfaces. These measurements accumulated by the system are transmitted wirelessly to an interactive website, where users can visualize environmental changes, compare historical trends, and evaluate their statistical significance.

By connecting satellite-based observations with ground-level measurements, our solution aims to make winter road conditions easier to understand while providing valuable localized data for researchers and transportation authorities. Ultimately, our goal is simple: to help communities better understand the roads they rely on and make every winter journey a little safer.

We used SI to help us understand and analyze the data, and explain changes in weather conditions more clearly.
details:
How does it work:

  1. Long-term data: NASA CDO daily temperatures, going back about 43 winters, for five Ontario sites. We compute freezing degree-days (FDD), meaning the accumulated cold that grows ice.
  2. Trend statistics: Using the previous year NASA data and our current real time data, we are able to look at various trends and the statistics and we can use it to explain regional climate changes. Every site shows a verdict computed from the data.
  3. Ice model: Stefan's law turns accumulated FDD into estimated ice thickness. Snow depth matters because snow insulates the ice, so we model its effect.
  4. Local field node: An Arduino with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (snow depth) and a DHT11 (temperature and humidity) sends a reading every ~2 seconds. A Raspberry Pi 4 with a screen shows everything.
  5. Nowcast fusion: The model combines NASA-verified data up to its latest date with our node's readings after it, and labels each part so you can see which is which.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

  • Improved Road Safety: Helps drivers stay informed about potentially hazardous winter road conditions.
  • Real-Time Monitoring: Provides up-to-date temperature, humidity, and estimated snow accumulation measurements.
  • Affordable Technology: Uses low-cost sensors and microcontrollers, making wider deployment more accessible.
  • Localized Accuracy: Collects measurements directly from specific locations rather than relying only on regional weather forecasts.
  • Environmental Research: Combines ground-level measurements with NASA data to support long-term environmental analysis.
  • Easy Data Access: Displays weather measurements, graphs, and trends on an interactive website.
  • Future Expansion: Could be deployed along highways to support road maintenance decisions and winter weather monitoring.

Tools, Coding languages, Hardware or software used to develop:

  1. Coding languages: Python, CSS, Typescript
  2. Hardware: Arduino, Raspberry pi 0W, Temperature and humidity sensor, Ultrasonic sensor, wires, breadboard, USB cable, screen
  3. Software: Arduino ID

How is our project is creative:

ColdCase is creative because it combines NASA's historical environmental data with real-time measurements from affordable sensors to monitor localized winter road conditions. Our website visualizes the data, identifies environmental trends, and evaluates their statistical significance.

What factors did our team take into consideration:

Our team focused on affordability, accuracy, accessibility, scalability, and road safety. We designed ColdCase with the goal of improving winter road monitoring in Northeastern Ontario while providing useful data for future environmental research.
